The Pacific bluefin tuna (Thunnus orientalis) is a large, highly migratory scombrid that ranges across the North Pacific Ocean, prized both ecologically as an apex pelagic predator and commercially as one of the most valuable food fishes in the world. Newly hatched larvae emerge at a total length at birth of just 0.308 centimeters [Lb = 0.308 centimeters], with larvae maintained at 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C] completing yolk absorption within days of hatching. This minute larval size reflects the small, pelagic eggs typical of scombrids, which broadcast enormous numbers of eggs into the open ocean.

Juvenile Pacific bluefin tuna grow at an exceptionally rapid pace, a trait that distinguishes tunas from most other teleost fishes and supports their highly active, endothermic lifestyle. This rapid early growth allows young tuna to quickly outgrow the size range most vulnerable to predation by other pelagic fishes, transitioning within their first year to a body plan capable of sustained high-speed swimming across vast oceanic distances.

Sexual maturation in this species is markedly delayed relative to its rapid juvenile growth. Individuals attain reproductive maturity at a total length at puberty of 150 centimeters [Lp = 150 centimeters], a substantial size reached only after several years of growth. The time since birth at first reproduction is approximately 1,170 days [tR = approximately 1,170 days] at the same reference temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], reflecting the considerable somatic investment required before this large-bodied migratory predator can allocate resources to reproduction.

Adults of the Pacific bluefin tuna ultimately attain an impressive total length of 265 centimeters [Li = 265 centimeters], among the largest sizes recorded for any tuna species. This immense adult body size supports the species' role as a dominant pelagic predator capable of pursuing fast-swimming prey such as sardines, anchovies, and squid across thousands of kilometers of open ocean during its extensive annual migrations.

Longevity in the Pacific bluefin tuna reaches a maximum of approximately 27 years [am = approximately 27 years] at 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], a considerable lifespan for a large pelagic scombrid. This extended longevity, combined with delayed maturity at 150 centimeters [Lp = 150 centimeters] and substantial ultimate size of 265 centimeters [Li = 265 centimeters], situates the species toward the slower end of the life-history continuum among tunas, a pattern that has historically rendered heavily fished populations particularly vulnerable to overexploitation.
